procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 13.02.2019 passed by the Secretary (Home), State of UP, Lucknow, ordering further investigation by CBCID of Case Crime No. 1069/2014.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The mother of the deceased, Satyveer alias Kallu, challenged the Secretary (Home)'s order in the High Court of Allahabad via Criminal Misc. Writ Petition No. 7093/2019. The High Court dismissed the writ petition, observing that the further investigation was ordered after intimation to the learned Magistrate and therefore, there is no infirmity in the order passed by the Secretary (Home) directing further investigation.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Feeling aggrieved and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court of Allahabad in Criminal Misc. Writ Petition No. 7093/2019, the original writ petitioner (mother of the deceased) preferred an appeal to the Supreme Court.

directions: The impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court is hereby quashed and set aside.

Order dated 13.02.2019 passed by the Secretary (Home), State of U.P., Lucknow ordered for reinvestigation by CBCID of Case Crime No. 1069/2014 under Sections 302 and 120B of IPC, Police Station Baraut, District, is hereby quashed and set aside.
Further investigation / reinvestigation by the CBCID is also hereby quashed and set aside.
All the defences which may be available to the accused are to be considered by the learned Trial Court at the time of trial.
Connected Criminal Appeal arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 7708/2021 filed by original accused Nos. 6 and 7 against issuance of non-bailable warrants against them stands dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order for reinvestigation by a different agency (CBCID) is legally valid without the prior permission of the Magistrate, especially after a chargesheet has been filed and cognizance has been taken.

facts: A chargesheet and a supplementary chargesheet were filed against the accused, and the Magistrate had taken cognizance of the offense.
The accused's attempts to quash the proceedings were dismissed by the High Court and the Supreme Court.
After a non-bailable warrant was issued, the mother of an accused applied to the Secretary (Home) for further investigation.
The Secretary (Home) ordered the investigation to be transferred to a different agency, the CBCID.
The CBCID then sent an "intimation" to the Magistrate about this order; no prior permission was sought or granted by the Magistrate.
law: The Court distinguished between "further investigation" and "reinvestigation."
For a "further investigation" by the original investigating officer, prior approval from the Magistrate is not required even after a chargesheet is filed.
However, for a "reinvestigation," especially by a different agency, the prior permission and approval of the Magistrate is mandatory.
An order for reinvestigation by another agency passed by the Secretary (Home) at the request of the accused's family is "unknown to law."
application: The Court determined that the transfer of the case to a new agency (CBCID) after chargesheets had already been filed constituted a "reinvestigation," not merely a "further investigation."
As it was a reinvestigation, the mandatory requirement of prior permission from the Magistrate was triggered.
The Court found that the CBCID merely sending an "intimation" to the Magistrate after the decision was already made does not satisfy the legal requirement for "prior permission/approval."
The Court explicitly rejected the High Court's finding that the order had the Magistrate's "concurrence," stating this was factually incorrect.
Furthermore, the Court held that the Secretary (Home) lacked the legal authority to order such a reinvestigation, rendering the initial order invalid.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the order for reinvestigation by the CBCID was legally invalid. It reasoned that this was a case of "reinvestigation" by a new agency, which requires the prior permission of the Magistrate. Since no such permission was obtained—only a subsequent intimation was sent—the process was legally flawed. The Court also found the order from the Secretary (Home) itself to be without legal authority.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is permissible to order a reinvestigation at the instance of an accused after a chargesheet has been filed, cognizance taken, and the accused's own petition to quash the proceedings has been dismissed by the High Court and the Supreme Court.

facts: A chargesheet was filed against the accused (Respondent Nos. 8 and 11) for murder, and the Magistrate took cognizance of it.
The accused's petition to quash the criminal proceedings and the chargesheet was dismissed by the High Court, and a subsequent appeal was also dismissed by the Supreme Court.
After a non-bailable warrant was issued, the mother of the accused applied to the Secretary (Home) for a reinvestigation.
The Secretary (Home) ordered a reinvestigation by a different agency (CBCID), which only sent an intimation to the Magistrate but did not obtain prior permission.
law: The Court distinguishes between 'further investigation' and 'reinvestigation'. While a further investigation under Section 173(8) Cr.PC does not require the Magistrate's prior approval, a reinvestigation, especially by a different agency, requires the prior permission of the Magistrate.

Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (ss. 173(3) r/w s. 158), the power to investigate or further investigate lies with the officer in charge of the concerned police station or their superior officer.
An executive authority like the Secretary (Home) has no power under the law to order a reinvestigation.
The proper legal remedy for an accused aggrieved by a chargesheet is to file a quashing petition (u/s 482 Cr.PC) or a discharge application before the appropriate court.
application: The Court classified the action ordered by the Secretary (Home) as a 'reinvestigation' by a new agency, not merely a 'further investigation'.
As it was a reinvestigation, the prior permission of the Magistrate was mandatory, but it was not obtained. The mere intimation sent to the Magistrate was not legally sufficient.
The Court found that the order passed by the Secretary (Home) was 'unknown to law' because the official lacked the statutory authority to order a reinvestigation.

The Court held that allowing the accused to obtain a reinvestigation through an executive authority after failing to get the chargesheet quashed by the High Court and Supreme Court would be an improper circumvention of the established judicial process.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that it is not permissible to order a reinvestigation at the instance of an accused after a chargesheet has been filed, cognizance has been taken, and the accused's own petition to quash the proceedings has been dismissed by the highest courts. The Court reasoned that such an order, especially from an executive authority like the Secretary (Home), is without legal basis and allows the accused to improperly bypass the judicial process to nullify a valid chargesheet. Therefore, the order for reinvestigation was quashed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order for reinvestigation by a different agency (CBCID) is legally valid without the prior permission of the Magistrate, especially after a chargesheet has been filed and cognizance has been taken.
appellant_arguments: The High Court materially erred in observing that the reinvestigation was ordered with the concurrence of the Magistrate.
No leave or permission was sought from or granted by the Magistrate for the reinvestigation; there was only an intimation, which is not legally sufficient.
respondent_arguments: Investigation by another agency is permissible under Section 173(3) read with Section 158 of the Cr.PC.

After the CBCID investigation, a further report will be submitted, and it is ultimately for the Magistrate to consider all three reports (original chargesheet, supplementary chargesheet, and the new report) before making a decision.

arguments.issue_text: Whether it is permissible to order a reinvestigation at the instance of an accused after a chargesheet has been filed, cognizance taken, and the accused's own petition to quash the proceedings has been dismissed by the High Court and the Supreme Court.
appellant_arguments: The High Court failed to appreciate that the accused's petition to quash the criminal proceedings and the chargesheet had already been dismissed by both the High Court and the Supreme Court.
The grounds on which the investigation was transferred are essentially the defenses of the accused, which should be considered at trial, not through a reinvestigation.
Ordering a reinvestigation at this stage would virtually acquit the chargesheeted accused and nullify the existing chargesheet, which is not permissible.
respondent_arguments: A further report from the new investigation will be submitted to the Magistrate, who can then consider all available reports, ensuring a comprehensive review of the evidence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Reinvestigation of a case requires the prior permission or approval of the Magistrate; a mere intimation to the Magistrate does not satisfy this requirement.
obiter: An investigating officer has the right to conduct further investigation in respect of an offence even after a chargesheet has been filed, and the prior approval of the Magistrate is not required for such further investigation.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The order for reinvestigation by the CBCID is legally invalid because it is not a 'further investigation' but a 'reinvestigation' by a different agency, which requires prior permission from the Magistrate, a condition not met in this case. The High Court was factually incorrect to state the Magistrate had concurred; the record shows only an intimation was sent, which is not legally sufficient. Furthermore, ordering such a reinvestigation at the behest of an accused's mother, after a chargesheet has been filed, cognizance taken, and the accused's own quashing petition has been dismissed, is a procedure 'un-known to law' and improperly allows the accused to introduce trial defenses to nullify the existing chargesheet.
legal_tests_applied: As per the settled position of law, so far as the reinvestigation is concerned, the prior permission/approval of the Magistrate is required.
An 'intimation' to the learned Magistrate cannot be considered as the 'concurrence' of the learned Magistrate.
policy_considerations: The grounds on which the investigation was transferred are essentially the defenses of the accused, which are required to be considered at the time of trial, not through a reinvestigation.

Ordering a reinvestigation at the instance of an accused after a chargesheet has been filed and cognizance taken would 'virtually acquit the accused' and 'tantamount to nullify the chargesheet,' which is not permissible.
An executive authority ordering a reinvestigation based on a complaint from an accused's family, after the judicial process is already underway, is a procedure 'un-known to law'.
